title: The Supply Side of Social Media
abstract: We trace the prevalence of politically extreme and envy-inducing content on social media to social media’s distinctive model of content production. Unlike legacy media outlets, which professionally procure small amounts of content, social media platforms rely on large numbers of predominantly unpaid users supplying content they are intrinsically motivated to produce, and use the resulting production scale to separately cherry-pick the pieces of content that most appeal to each viewer. Collecting observational data and conducting experiments with creators and viewers on Instagram, TikTok, X/Twitter, and YouTube, we show that because creators are not paid, content production is dominated by an unrepresentative minority of users who post enviable “lifestyle” content and extreme political content in pursuit of social status and expressive satisfaction. Post-by-post, enviable or extreme posts are not more likely than benign posts to highly engage a given viewer. But the scale at which enviable and extreme content is produced allows platforms to find a greater number of such posts that will appeal to a given user, due to closely matching the viewer’s interests on other dimensions. The prevalence of negative content on social media hence stems partly from platforms’ reliance on cheaply generating scale through status-, emotion-, and conflict-motivated production.
